items.title: UK GDPR, Article 35: Data protection impact assessment
items.quote: at least when there is a change of the risk represented by processing operations
items.why: The binding UK rule nearest to this question: the controller must review whether processing matches its impact assessment at least when the risk changes. Applies only where personal data and a high-risk assessment are involved.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: What do we need to know about accuracy and statistical accuracy?
items.locator: Section 'How should we define and prioritise different statistical accuracy measures?' (closing paragraphs on concept / model drift); section 'What should we do about statistical accuracy post-deployment?', first paragraph
items.quote: After deployment, you should implement monitoring, the frequency of which should be proportional to the impact an incorrect output may have on individuals.
items.why: Source of the quotation. The regulator also says 'You should regularly assess drift and retrain the model on new data where necessary' and expects documented thresholds for deciding when to retrain. Its example: if the skills a job needs change every two years, reassess at least that often. The page carries the notice that the guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act.

items.title: Data protection impact assessments: How do we do a DPIA?
items.locator: Section 'Step 7: How do we conclude our DPIA?', final paragraph (keep under review)
items.quote: You may need to repeat it if there is a substantial change to the nature, scope, context or purposes of your processing.
items.why: The trigger for an out-of-cycle review in the regulator's words: a substantial change to what the processing is, covers or is for. The page carries the notice that the guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act. No date printed; page metadata gives 18 February 2026.

items.title: SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
items.locator: Principle 4.4 (a) to (e), pp.26-27; Principle 2.6(b)(iii) on vendor models, p.19
items.quote: Model monitoring should be conducted on an ongoing basis with a frequency determined by the model tier.
items.why: The most developed UK supervisory text on monitoring models in use: performance against thresholds, whether the model is used beyond its intended use, analysis of overrides, independently reviewed reports, and the firm's own monitoring of vendor models. Applies to banks, building societies and designated investment firms with internal model approval; others 'may find the proposed principles useful'.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 9: Risk management system
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating
items.why: The clearest statutory statement that risk is not assessed once. A provider duty for high-risk systems; point (c) feeds in data from post-market monitoring. Article 9 is not marked amended. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 72: Post-market monitoring by providers and post-market monitoring plan for high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data
items.why: The provider must collect and analyse performance data through the system's lifetime, including data from deployers, in a way proportionate to the risks. Amended paragraph 3: the Commission is to adopt guidance, including a template, on the monitoring plan by 2 September 2027. The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.locator: Art. 26(5), first sentence and second subparagraph
items.quote: Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use
items.why: The deployer's share of monitoring, and the duty to pass information back to the provider. Financial institutions are deemed to comply through their existing governance rules. Applies to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027 (Article 113, read in the same copy). The Commission's copy of the consolidated text; the page states it is based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026 and marks Digital Omnibus changes NEW or AMENDED. EU law; not UK law.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Table 4, MANAGE 4.1, p.33 (PDF page 38); Table 1, GOVERN 1.5, p.23 (PDF page 28); Appendix B, p.38 (PDF page 43)
items.quote: maintenance due to data, model, or concept drift
items.why: International comparator, voluntary. Asks for post-deployment monitoring plans, a set frequency of periodic review with roles defined, and notes that AI systems may need more frequent maintenance and triggers for it. US framework with no legal force in the UK.

items.title: The Orange Book: Management of Risk, Principles and Concepts
items.publisher: HM Treasury and Government Finance Function
items.locator: Section D, 'Risk monitoring', paragraphs D10 and D11, pp.23-24 (PDF pages 25-26)
items.quote: Monitoring should play a role before, during and after implementation of risk treatment.
items.why: General UK risk practice: ongoing monitoring should show whether and how the risk profile is changing and whether controls work as intended, and results should feed performance reporting. Written for central government; not binding on companies.

items.title: A pro-innovation approach to AI regulation (white paper)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Section 3.2.3, principle 'Safety, security and robustness', definition and rationale
items.quote: function reliably as intended throughout their entire life cycle
items.why: Government policy, not law: regulators may require that AI systems are secure and reliable through their whole life cycle and that those involved 'regularly test or carry out due diligence'. Published under a previous government; no new rights or duties.

items.title: Temporal quality degradation in AI models
items.publisher: Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio); authors Daniel Vela, Andrew Sharp, Richard Zhang, Trang Nguyen, An Hoang and Oleg S. Pianykh
items.quote: we observed temporal model degradation in 91% of cases
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open-access evidence for why risk has to be looked at again after go-live: across 128 pairings of four standard model types with 32 datasets from healthcare operations, transport, finance and weather, quality fell with time since training in 91%. The nearest thing found to a defensible figure for this criterion. Limits: time-series prediction models, not language models; not UK data; the datasets were chosen by the authors, so the percentage describes their sample, not all AI systems.

items.title: How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?
items.publisher: arXiv (authors' copy; later published in Harvard Data Science Review); authors Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou
items.quote: when and how these models are updated over time is opaque
items.why: Evidence that a bought-in AI service can change without the customer being told: the same two services, tested in March and June 2023, gave markedly different results on the same tasks, better on some and worse on others. Supports a review trigger for supplier model changes and the authors' call for continuous monitoring. Limits: two products from one supplier over three months; the arXiv copy is cited because the journal's own page refused automated access; findings are dated.

items.title: FCA Handbook, PRIN 2A.9: Monitoring of consumer outcomes
items.quote: A firm must regularly monitor the outcomes retail customers receive from
items.why: A binding UK rule requiring continuing monitoring of results, not of documents: firms must regularly monitor the outcomes customers receive, be able to tell whether any group is getting worse outcomes than another, find root causes and act. It applies however the outcome is produced, so it covers AI used in retail financial services. Limits: FCA-authorised firms serving retail customers only; not AI-specific; frequency is left to the firm.

items.title: The Medical Devices (Post-market Surveillance Requirements) (Amendment) (Great Britain) Regulations 2024, regulation 4 (new Part 4A)
items.locator: Regulation 4, inserted regulation 44ZE(1) to (4); regulation 44ZF (surveillance plan)
items.quote: includes the analysis of data relevant to the quality, performance and safety of the device throughout its lifetime
items.why: UK legislation that makes lifecycle monitoring a legal duty for one class of AI: a manufacturer must keep a post-market surveillance system for each device, proportionate to its risk, covering its whole lifetime, and use the data to update its risk analysis and to spot trends in incidents. Limits: manufacturers of medical devices only, not users; Great Britain; the as-made text; later amendments not checked.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 12 'Monitor your system’s behaviour', provisions 12.2 and 12.4
items.quote: monitor the performance of their models and system over time so that they can detect sudden or gradual changes in behaviour
items.why: The UK government code's monitoring principle, addressed to organisations that deploy AI as well as those that build it: analyse logs to confirm the system still produces the desired outputs and to detect drift or unexpected behaviour, and watch performance over time. Limits: voluntary; written for security, so it frames change in behaviour as a security concern.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 5: 'You understand how to manage the full AI life cycle'
items.quote: You should understand how to monitor and mitigate for potential drift, bias, and, in the case of generative AI, hallucinations.
items.why: Current UK government guidance to its own departments: an AI system has a full life cycle to manage, with a robust testing and monitoring process in place to catch drift and bias, and a plan for updating the system and closing it down. Limits: guidance for the public sector, not binding on companies; principles, not a monitoring method.

items.title: AI tools in recruitment: audit outcomes report
items.locator: Section 'Accuracy, fairness, and bias mitigation in AI', findings on accuracy testing
items.quote: The majority of AI providers repeated accuracy tests at least periodically after launch and especially before implementing changes or updates.
items.why: What the UK regulator found when it audited real AI suppliers: most retested accuracy after launch and before changes so that it 'did not erode over time', but its example is a provider that had not formally assessed accuracy before launch. The regulator assessed whether providers 'regularly monitored accuracy and bias' through the lifecycle. Limits: consensual audits of recruitment-tool developers and providers between August 2023 and May 2024; a snapshot; gives no counts.
